name: gnuastro
desc: Astronomical data manipulation and analysis utilities and libraries
why: Real astronomy data analysis utilities you can run on actual telescope images at home.

brief.what_it_is: GNU Astronomy Utilities (Gnuastro) is an official GNU package of command-line programs and library functions for manipulating and analysing astronomical data. The programs share one common command-line interface. The homepage does not spell out the input and output formats in detail, but the programs are named after common FITS-image and table operations, such as arithmetic on images, convolution, cropping, warping, table handling, statistics, source detection (NoiseChisel), segmentation, and catalogue creation. The homepage describes the package as data manipulation and analysis utilities rather than a single tool. The homepage lists 27 executables, including astfits, asttable, astarithmetic, astnoisechisel, astmkprof and astquery.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage says Gnuastro is written to comply fully with the GNU coding standards so that it integrates with GNU/Linux, and that astronomers can expect a familiar experience in the source code, building, installing and command-line use they already know from other GNU software.
brief.how_it_works: Each program is a separate command-line tool that follows the same basic interface. Gnuastro has three mandatory dependencies: the GNU Scientific Library, CFITSIO and WCSLIB. The homepage says that the programs can be used from the shell, and that each has a full entry in the Info manual and a man page. It also says that every program accepts a --cite option that prints how to cite Gnuastro and that program.

brief.install_notes: The homepage lists Gnuastro as available from many OS package managers and from Conda. It names brew among the tools for installing dependencies, through the 'Dependencies from package managers' section. Building from source is possible. The homepage says the source tree must be bootstrapped before it can be configured and built, and that tarballs for the latest commit are available. The Gnuastro book's Installation chapter covers dependencies, downloads and build steps. The homepage gives no hardware, account or runtime requirements, and no first-run steps beyond the info and --help pointers.
brief.standout: The programs share one command-line interface and follow GNU coding standards, so they behave like other GNU tools. Each program has a built-in citation helper (--cite) that reports the correct paper for that program, which is unusual for scientific software.
brief.status: maintained. The homepage says the current stable release is Gnuastro 0.24, released on November 26th, 2025. It also says the project is still under active development, that new releases are announced on info-gnuastro, and that the manual page was last updated November 27, 2025. Maintainer: Mohammad Akhlaghi. The homepage also says the project is 11 years old as of 2026.
brief.caveats: The homepage does not give worked examples of running any program on real data. It lists three mandatory dependencies that must be installed first. Building the git version requires bootstrapping. The homepage says the test tarball changes with every commit and is not archived. The homepage says there is no single introductory paper yet, so citing it means citing the NoiseChisel paper or the paper for each program. The GNU homepage's own copyright and licence text is CC BY-ND 4.0 for the page; the software itself is GPL v3 or later. The brew caveat field was empty. The scout note calls this 'real astronomy data analysis utilities you can run on actual telescope images at home'. The homepage does not say anything specific about home use. Its own framing is about the GNU coding standards and the Unix interface.
quotes: GNU Astronomy Utilities (Gnuastro) is an official GNU package consisting of various programs and library functions for the manipulation and analysis of (astronomical) data.
All the programs share the same basic command-line user interface for the comfort of both the users and developers.
Gnuastro is written to comply fully with the GNU coding standards so it integrates finely with the GNU/Linux operating system.
There is no paper fully devoted to introducing Gnuastro yet (we are more focused on reaching the goals of version 1.0).

judge.reason: Gnuastro opens a real scientific rabbit hole: its astronomy-specific tools include NoiseChisel for finding sources in telescope images, not just generic file manipulation.

entry.title: Gnuastro
entry.tldr: An official GNU package of 27 command-line programs for astronomical images and tables, from cropping and warping to NoiseChisel source detection, all sharing one interface.
entry.deeper_look:
Gnuastro, the GNU Astronomy Utilities, is a set of separate command-line programs and library functions for manipulating and analysing astronomical data. The names point at familiar FITS-style operations: `astarithmetic` for arithmetic on images, `astconvolve`, `astcrop`, `astwarp`, `asttable`, `aststatistics`, plus `astnoisechisel` for detecting faint sources, `astsegment`, and `astmkcatalog` for building catalogues. There are also a number of `astscript-*` helpers, for example for radial profiles and PSF work.

The idea underneath it is that astronomy pipelines can be built the Unix way. Each program does one job, and all of them share the same basic command-line interface, so learning one teaches you the rest. The project follows the GNU coding standards so that building, installing and running it feels like any other GNU software. In its own words, "All the programs share the same basic command-line user interface for the comfort of both the users and developers."

Documentation is the way in. The whole book is available through `info gnuastro`, each program has its own Info entry and man page, and every program accepts `--cite`, which prints how to cite Gnuastro and that particular program. That is a small but rare nicety in scientific software.

The project is about eleven years old and still under active development. The current stable release is 0.24, from November 2025.
entry.install:
brew install gnuastro
# Pulls in the required libraries: cfitsio, gsl and wcslib, plus a few others. You will need FITS images of your own to do anything real with it.

Opens the complete Gnuastro book in Info format, starting from the beginning.
Shows the 'Invoking' section of the manual for the cropping program.

entry.whats_unique: Real observational-astronomy tooling packaged as a polite GNU citizen: one shared interface across every program, a book-length Info manual, and a built-in `--cite` option on each tool.
entry.caveats: The homepage gives no worked examples on real data, so you need your own FITS files and the manual to get anywhere, and there is still no single introductory paper to cite.
